common_name: Silberperle Korean Fir (Silver Pearl Dwarf Korean Fir)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic soil, choosing a site with some shelter from harsh afternoon sun.

directions: Silberperle is an ultra-slow, globose dwarf selection of Korean fir whose short, densely packed needles curl upward to show their bright white undersides, giving the whole mound a frosted, pearly cast. Expect only an inch or two of growth per year, so give it a permanent, uncrowded spot in a rock garden or conifer collection rather than a bed that gets reworked often. Grow it in well-drained, evenly moist, slightly acidic soil and avoid heavy clay or waterlogged sites, which this fir will not tolerate. Light afternoon shade in hot climates helps prevent needle scorch while still keeping the form tight and dense.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in deep, well-drained soil; give it room to spread flat rather than crowding it against other dwarf conifers.

directions: Arne's Dwarf forms a low, flat-topped, broadly spreading mound of dense, glossy dark-green needles, growing wider than it is tall over many years. It stays compact without pruning, making it a dependable anchor shrub for foreground conifer plantings or larger rock gardens. Plant in deep, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, since Nordmann fir resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought. Once established it needs very little maintenance beyond removing any upright reversion shoots that occasionally appear from the graft.

planting.note: Set out in spring into well-drained soil; treat as a long-term miniature feature rather than a filler plant, since it barely changes size from year to year.

directions: Originating as a witch's-broom mutation, Shadow's Broom is one of the slowest-growing oriental spruce selections available, forming a tight, irregular miniature mound of short dark-green needles that may take decades to exceed a foot in height. Because growth is measured in fractions of an inch per year, it is best suited to trough gardens, miniature conifer collections, or bonsai-style container culture. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil, since this spruce does poorly with wet feet, and avoid overcrowding it with faster-growing neighbors that will shade it out. Winter protection from drying wind helps keep the dense foliage from browning in exposed sites.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in an open, sunny position with room for a slowly thickening globe.

directions: Howell's Dwarf is a compact, rounded selection of the uncommon Alcock's spruce, carrying the species' distinctive blue-green needles with silvery undersides on a dense, slow-growing globe. It is a good choice for collectors wanting an unusual spruce texture without the eventual bulk of the species form, which can reach sizeable tree proportions. Grow it in full sun and well-drained soil, and avoid sites with standing winter water, which spruce roots do not tolerate. Minimal pruning is needed; just remove any stray vigorous shoots to keep the globose outline even.

planting.note: Set out in spring or early fall into cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil with some protection from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Jervis is a dense, globose dwarf hemlock that builds a tight mound of short, fine-textured needles and holds its compact habit with essentially no shaping required. Like all hemlocks it prefers cool, consistently moist, well-drained soil and benefits from afternoon shade in warm climates, where foliage can bronze or scorch in full sun. It is well suited to rock gardens, trough plantings, and foreground spots in conifer collections where its small, slow-building shape won't be overtaken by neighbors. Avoid hot, dry, exposed sites and heavy wet clay alike; a humus-amended, evenly moist loam gives the best results.

planting.note: Plant small container stock in spring in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil; a raised bed or trough makes maintenance easiest given its tiny ultimate size.

directions: Minikin is one of the smallest named hemlock selections in cultivation, forming a tight, rounded cushion of short, densely set needles that advances only a fraction of an inch each year. It is best grown in a trough, raised rock garden, or miniature conifer collection where it will not be overtopped by faster plants. Provide cool, evenly moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil and afternoon shade in warmer zones to prevent needle browning. Because growth is so slow, this is a long-term specimen plant rather than one chosen for quick garden impact.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with some relief from the harshest midday sun.

directions: Named for the French garden where it was selected, Kerdalo is a slow-growing, broadly conical Hinoki cypress whose new spring growth emerges golden before settling into rich green, giving the plant a two-toned glow each season. It keeps a neat, dense outline with little pruning and works well as a textured accent among other dwarf conifers or in a mixed evergreen border. Grow it in evenly moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and shelter it from the most intense afternoon sun, which can bleach the foliage in hot climates. Avoid soggy or compacted ground, which weakens the fine surface roots typical of Hinoki cypress.

common_name: Silberspitz Atlas Cedar (Silver Tips Atlas Cedar)

planting.note: Plant in spring into dry-to-moderate, sharply drained soil in full sun; avoid low spots that collect winter moisture.

directions: Silberspitz is a compact, slow-growing Atlas cedar whose new candles of growth emerge creamy-white to silver before maturing to blue-green, giving the whole plant a frosted, two-toned look through the growing season. It builds an irregular, somewhat conical form over time and suits sunny, well-drained slopes or Mediterranean-style plantings better than damp, heavy soils. Water sparingly once established, since Atlas cedar is markedly drought-tolerant and prone to root problems in wet ground. Choose a sheltered site in colder parts of its range, as the silvery new growth can be damaged by harsh, drying winter wind.
